cases.abstract: FlexGen targets bulk language-model generation when weights and key-value caches exceed GPU memory. Reusing each loaded layer across blocks of batches amortizes weight transfers; offloading caches as well as weights permits larger batches than weight-only offloading. A cost model and linear-programming search select placements across GPU, CPU, and disk and batch sizes. Without CPU computation and neglecting activation I/O, the implemented schedule has asymptotic weight I/O within twice optimal. On synthetic OPT-175B generation with 512-token prompts and 32-token outputs, a 16-GB T4 with 208-GB host memory and SSD achieves 0.69 generated tokens/s, versus 0.01 for unquantized Accelerate and DeepSpeed, supporting throughput-oriented offloading beyond model fitting. Group-wise 4-bit weight/cache compression avoids disk swapping and raises throughput to 1.12 tokens/s without retraining or calibration. These benchmarks use dummy weights; separate real-weight Lambada and WikiText tests show small quality changes with 4-bit compression and sparse value-cache loading, whereas 3-bit compression does not preserve accuracy. Compression is not uniformly faster. Four-GPU pipelining yields superlinear decoding scaling but sublinear total-generation scaling for OPT-30B and OPT-175B with 32-token outputs. The gains depend on host memory and favor bulk throughput over low-latency generation.
cases.notes: Connected cache offloading and layer reuse to attainable batching, so the same-hardware throughput comparison answers practical bulk-generation efficiency rather than mere model fit (Sections 4 and 6.1). Retained the conditional scheduling bound, compression/sparse-attention quality evidence, and mixed compression/scaling outcomes. Tables 2 and 5 concern distinct dummy-weight and real-weight experiments; compression avoids disk swapping in the reported OPT-175B configuration. Table 3 separates decoding from total generation. The comparison supports the combined system, not an isolated causal attribution to scheduling.

cases.abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations parameterize hidden-state evolution continuously and obtain outputs with a black-box ODE solver. Adjoint training solves an augmented ODE backward, reconstructing states instead of storing solver operations, so memory is independent of function-evaluation count. Solver tolerances trade numerical accuracy for computation. On MNIST, an ODE network reaches 0.42% test error with 0.22 million parameters, versus 0.41% with 0.60 million for a residual network: continuous-depth training retains comparable classification performance with fewer parameters. For dynamics uniformly Lipschitz in state and continuous in time, an instantaneous change-of-variables theorem makes log-density evolution depend on a Jacobian trace instead of a determinant. Because traces add across additive dynamics, continuous normalizing flows can widen with density-update cost linear in hidden-unit count; toy experiments illustrate reversible sampling and density estimation. A latent generative model uses shared dynamics to define trajectories at arbitrary observation times and incorporates Poisson likelihoods for observation timing. With 30 irregularly sampled observations from synthetic spirals, predictive RMSE is 0.1642 versus 0.3937 for an RNN, supporting extrapolation from irregular observations using continuous latent dynamics. Backward reconstruction can introduce numerical error; checkpointing trades storage for reconstruction accuracy.
cases.notes: Connected backward state reconstruction to the memory saving, and trace additivity to widening flows. MNIST tests whether continuous-depth training preserves classification performance with fewer parameters; the synthetic spiral comparison tests irregular-time extrapolation, not real-world deployment. Preserved latent trajectories and observation-time likelihoods as co-contributions, alongside flow density modeling. CNF/NF density-matching optimizers and iteration budgets differ (Section 4.1), so toy results illustrate capabilities rather than matched-budget superiority. The constant-memory claim remains conditional on backward reconstruction, whose numerical error motivates checkpointing (Section 6).
